effect_mechanism: Mangrove belts strongly reduce coastal flooding by breaking waves and, more weakly, lowering surge water as it passes through the forest [ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_1, ev_flood_hazard_gijsman21_3]. A global model finds that losing current mangroves would flood 28% more people each year [ev_flood_hazard_menendez20_1], and a Philippine model gives 24% more [ev_flood_hazard_wbphl17_1]. In India and Bangladesh, villages sheltered by existing mangrove forest took less salt water and flood water after super cyclones [ev_flood_hazard_badola05_7, ev_flood_hazard_akber18_7]. The avoided damage has been put in money terms: in Orissa mangroves protected houses worth USD 1218 per hectare of forest in a single cyclone [ev_economic_return_das11_1], and mangroves in front of sea dykes cut repair costs by 20–30% [ev_avoided_damage_value_badola05_10]. effect_mechanism: The evidence points to a small production gain, though the support is weak, mostly in pond farming next to the mangroves. A World Bank project report in Viet Nam cites studies finding that improved mangrove forest more than 5 years old raised aquaculture values by US$359.7/ha and US$276.6/ha, and by US$1,436.8/ha/year in a third study [ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_5, ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_6]. A Senegal model assumes mangrove restoration raises farm productivity by 2.3% [ev_crop_yield_iisd26_5]. Other findings point the other way, for pond farming. In northern Java, Indonesia, the authors judge that mangroves planted on pond walls and inside ponds hamper pond upkeep, and that their leaf litter and shade lower pond yield [ev_aquaculture_yield_bosma20_2]. In the Philippines, a study citing earlier work notes that turning leased brackish fishponds back into mangrove gives up their fish output (these ponds average 1.06 t/ha), although the cited author judges the national loss small and easily replaced [ev_aquaculture_yield_ferrer11_2].
conditionality: Both pond findings say mangroves in ponds, or in place of ponds, lower pond yield [ev_aquaculture_yield_bosma20_2, ev_aquaculture_yield_ferrer11_2]. No study here measures pond yield with and without mangroves at a similar level of farming intensity, so the size of that loss is unknown. None of the gains is measured at a project site either: the Viet Nam figures are values borrowed from other studies, and the Senegal figure is a model assumption [ev_agricultural_production_value_wbicr6719_6, ev_crop_yield_iisd26_5]. The Indonesian finding is the authors' judgement and the Philippine one is second-hand. What separates the sides is where the mangroves are: beside the ponds in the Viet Nam figures, inside or instead of them in the Indonesian and Philippine findings.
